subsection.p: The most common mistakes come from forgetting one of these meanings. A definite integral is signed accumulation. An indefinite integral is a family of functions. A substitution changes both the integrand and the limits. A formula for an antiderivative must be valid on the interval where it is used.

subsection.title: Skills: FTC and substitution
subsection.p: The following problems are meant to build fluency. In each problem, first identify which idea is being used: FTC Part I, FTC Part II, an indefinite integral, substitution, or orientation.

paragraphs.title: A. Differentiate accumulation functions
paragraphs.p: Assume all integrands are continuous on the relevant intervals. Find the derivative.

li.p: M(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x |t|\,dt. Where is M differentiable, and what is M'(x)?

paragraphs.title: B. Evaluate definite integrals
paragraphs.p: Use antiderivatives and the Fundamental Theorem, Part II.

li.p: \displaystyle\int_{-2}^2 (x^3+4x)\,dx. Explain why the answer could have been predicted from symmetry.

paragraphs.title: C. Indefinite integrals and initial values
paragraphs.p: Find the family of antiderivatives. Then solve the initial value problems.

li.p: Solve s'(t)=3t^2-12t+9, \qquad s(0)=5. Then find s(4)-s(0).
A population changes at the rate P'(t)=20e^{0.1t} people per year. If P(0)=500, find P(t).
A temperature changes at the rate T'(t)=-6e^{-0.2t} degrees Celsius per minute. If T(0)=80, find T(t).

paragraphs.title: D. Substitution
paragraphs.p: Use substitution. For definite integrals, change the limits or clearly return to the original variable before using the original limits.

li.p: \displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}2xe^{x^2}\,dx. Explain how the substitution handles the orientation.
Let F(x)=\displaystyle\int_1^x \frac{1}{t}\,dt, \qquad x\gt 0. Find F'(x). What familiar function has the same derivative and the same value at x=1?
Let A(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x (2+t)\,dt. Find A(x) by evaluating the integral. Then differentiate your formula and check FTC Part I.
Let B(x)=\displaystyle\int_x^{x^2} t^2\,dt. Find B'(x) using moving endpoints. Then evaluate B(x) explicitly and check your derivative.

subsection.title: Concept checks
subsection.p: Answer in complete sentences where appropriate.

li.p: What is the difference between \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx and \displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx?
In A(x)=\displaystyle\int_a^x f(t)\,dt, why do we usually use t instead of x inside the integral?
State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part I, in words.
State the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part II, in words.
Why does FTC Part I require continuity at the point where we take the derivative?
If F'(x)=f(x), why do all antiderivatives of f on one interval have the form F(x)+C?
Why does the constant C disappear when we use an antiderivative to evaluate a definite integral?
Give an example where \displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=0 but the ordinary area between the graph and the x-axis is not 0.
If v(t) is velocity, what is the difference between \displaystyle\int_a^b v(t)\,dt and \displaystyle\int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt?
Why must the limits change when we use a substitution in a definite integral?
Suppose u=x^2. If x goes from 1 to 3, what are the corresponding u-limits?
Suppose u=1-x. If x goes from 0 to 1, what are the corresponding u-limits? What does this have to do with orientation?
Why is it dangerous to use -\frac1x as an antiderivative for 1/x^2 across an interval containing 0?

subsection.title: Project: reconstruct a function from its rate
subsection.p: A rate tells how a quantity changes. The Fundamental Theorem tells how to rebuild the quantity from the rate, once one starting value is known.
This project reconstructs a quantity from both an exact rate formula and sampled rate data.

note.title: What the project tests
note.p: A rate graph is not the same thing as the quantity graph. The rate tells the slope of the quantity. The quantity is reconstructed by accumulation.
